lines: Someone wants a dashboard, so they point a script straight at the controller's own tags and start asking for a few thousand of them every second.
Not long after, the controller's own loop starts running behind, and a conveyor on the line faults.
Nothing was ever written to that controller. The asking itself was enough.
That's not an accident of one careless script. The floor is built this way on purpose.
A plant's network is split into levels, with a buffer zone standing between the office network and the one that actually runs production.
Any path a data platform takes to pull a reading off that floor has to cross that boundary somewhere, and where it crosses is a real decision, not a formality.
Here's the question worth sitting with before the next reveal answers it.
That script never once wrote a value back to the controller. It only asked for readings.
Can a request that never writes anything still disturb the process being controlled?
answer: It can, and that's the whole surprise.
A controller's own loop has to answer every outside request on top of running its actual control logic.
Ask it for enough at once, and the answering itself starts eating into the time that loop needed for the job it was actually built to do.

lines: Put a real number on it.
Asking a controller rated to handle a few hundred such requests each second for several thousand, once a second, is several times more than it was ever budgeted to carry.
That gap shows up before a single reading has even changed.
The obvious next move is to stop asking for everything on a fixed clock and only ask to be told when a value actually changes.
That one change cuts the load by more than half.
And it still doesn't fit inside this plant's own stated budget. The obvious fix wasn't enough on its own.
So change what's being asked, not how often.
Read the same values from whatever already keeps its own running archive of them, or from a copy built for exactly this purpose, instead of going back to the controller at all.
The controller's own share of the load drops to nothing it has to carry. The fix was never about asking less often. It was about asking something else entirely.
One more piece has to hold even once the reading is flowing somewhere safe to ask.
Put a bounded holding area between whatever is pulling those readings and whatever consumes them downstream, and let that holding area fill up.
Once it's full, it quietly lets go of its own oldest item to make room for the newest one. The side doing the asking never once gets told to wait.
None of this works unless everyone agrees on who's actually in charge of which copy of the data.
The controller's own value, the running archive, and the production system's own record all belong to the engineering side that keeps the floor running.
The copy that ends up stored for analysis belongs to a different team entirely.
Here's the part that's easy to miss: the meaning of a field, not just its bytes, still belongs to whoever owned it on the floor, no matter which team's system the bytes end up living in.
Now watch what happens when something on the floor changes without anyone downstream being told.
A sensor gets re-scaled after a firmware update, and its name on the floor changes along with it.

A reader that only ever knew the old name quietly stops seeing anything new at all, while a reader that was told in advance to expect both names keeps reading straight through the change without missing a single value.
A floor that's segmented on purpose, not by accident.
A request that never writes anything can still cost more than it was ever budgeted to cost.
The actual fix is asking something built to carry that load, not asking the controller less often.
A holding area protects the side doing the asking, never the other way around.
Who owns a copy of the data, and who owns what a field even means, are two separate questions with two separate, assigned answers.
And a name change on the floor only breaks the reader nobody warned in advance.
One more case to reason through before moving on.
A new consumer wants to be told about tag changes straight from the controller's own interface, the moment they happen, rather than going through anything built to carry that load.
Is that the same risk as the earlier script that just asked for everything on a fixed clock?
answer: It is, even though it feels much lighter than the earlier script.
The controller still has to do the work of deciding whether each value actually changed before it can tell anyone about it.
That work is exactly what was costing time in the first place, so the same budget question still applies, with a smaller number in it, not a different question entirely.
